note: Row set is correct and complete: 25 rows, one per game year 2001-2025 (SB XXXV-LIX). No rows added or removed. Rebuilt every column independently. The defect is confined to the two Nielsen columns, and it is a BASIS inconsistency. Nielsen publishes a single 'Historical Super Bowl Audience Data - U.S. Television Audience Estimates' table (identical in its Feb-2024 LVIII and Feb-2025 LIX releases) giving, per game, combined Total Viewers P2+ and combined HHLD Rating across every carrying network and streaming platform, inclusive of out-of-home and digital - exactly the two quantities this question asks for. The gold's HHLD column already matches that Nielsen table in 24/25 rows (including the distinctive 43.5 for 2024, which is the all-network combined rating vs 42.1 CBS-only, and 41.4/42.0/38.4/37.9/40.7 for 2019-2023), proving the Nielsen table is the gold's own intended basis. But the gold's viewership column silently switches basis in 10 rows: it uses single-network Nielsen figures for 2014-2018 (111.5/114.4/111.9/111.3/103.4 instead of the combined 112.8/114.8/112.3/112.0/104.0), NBC's disputed self-reported 'total audience delivery' claim of 112.3 for 2022 (Nielsen: 101.5), CBS's pre-restatement 96.4 for 2021 (Nielsen: 95.9), stale unrounded values for 2005 (86.0 vs 86.1) and 2008 (97.5 vs 97.4), and for 2019 it uses 98.2, which is not the game audience at all but the average HALFTIME SHOW audience. Patched all 10 viewership cells plus one rating cell (2008: 43.3 -> 43.1; 43.3 is the 2000 SB XXXIV value, and Nielsen and Wikipedia both give 43.1 for SB XLII). 11 cells corrected in total, all in 11 distinct rows; the other 14 rows are unchanged. The patched viewership column reproduces the gold's 14 already-correct viewership cells exactly, which is independent confirmation the Nielsen table is the right source. Preserved the gold's formatting conventions: game-year in the Year column, contemporary stadium names, one decimal for viewership, and the gold's dropped trailing zero on integral ratings (42, 45, 46). recheck_note: All 11 changed cells confirmed correct; 0 disputed. I built the reference series myself before reading the auditor's case: curled the raw HTML of Nielsen's LIX release and regex-parsed the 'Historical Super Bowl Audience Data' table out of it (62 <tr> rows) rather than trusting a summarizer, then cross-checked the Feb-2024 LVIII release, which carries byte-identical values for every year in scope. CENTRAL BASIS CLAIM HOLDS, and it survives a discriminating test the auditor did not run. I isolated the years where Nielsen's combined all-network rating diverges from the single-network rating in Wikipedia's Super_Bowl_television_ratings (fetched as raw wikitext): 2019 (41.4 vs 41.1), 2020 (42.0 vs 41.6), 2021 (38.4 vs 38.2), 2022 (37.9 vs 36.9), 2023 (40.7 vs 40.4), 2024 (43.5 vs 42.1). The gold's rating column matches Nielsen-combined in 6/6 and single-network in 0/6; overall the gold's ratings match Nielsen in 24/25 rows (2008 the lone break). A SECOND independent test inside the viewership column itself: 2023 gold 115.1 = Nielsen 115,096,000, not single-network 114.21; 2024 gold 123.7 = Nielsen 123,714,000, not single-network 120.25. So the viewership column is already Nielsen-combined wherever it is right, which makes the 2014-2018 cells genuine internal inconsistencies rather than a different intended series. Competing bases ruled out: single-network fails the 6 rating years plus 2023/2024 viewership; self-reported 'total audience delivery' explains only 2 of 25 rows (2021 CBS 96.4, 2022 NBC 112.3) and is contradicted by 2019 (gold 98.2, not CBS's 100.7 all-platform claim) and 2024 (gold 123.7 = Nielsen); halftime-show audience explains nothing. Per cell, against the raw Nielsen table: 2005 86,072,000->86.1 (gold 86.0 truncated); 2008 rating 43.1 (gold's 43.3 is SB XXXIV/2000, sitting one row below XLII in the same Nielsen table); 2008 97,448,000->97.4 (gold's 97.5 is double-rounding of Wikipedia's pre-rounded 97.45; ESPN independently cites '97.4 million' for XLII); 2014 112,752,000->112.8; 2015 114,810,000->114.8; 2016 112,336,000->112.3; 2017 111,973,000->112.0; 2018 104,016,000->104.0; 2019 98,950,000->99.0; 2021 95,877,000->95.9; 2022 101,470,000->101.5. TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE AUDITOR'S REASONING that do not change any cell value: (a) the 2019 claim that gold's 98.2 is 'the average HALFTIME SHOW audience' is FALSE - 98.2M is the contemporaneous CBS-only game average, per Nielsen's own Feb-2019 post titled 'Super Bowl LIII Draws 98.2 Million TV Viewers' and matching ESPN/TVLine; right cell, wrong rationale. (b) 2014's 111.5 is not a single-network figure either - it is Nielsen's superseded fast-national preliminary (Nielsen's own Feb-2014 post 'Super Bowl XLVIII Draws 111.5 Million Viewers'), later revised to 112.2M final single-network and restated to 112,752,000 combined; it matches no current basis, which only strengthens the patch. GRADING-IMPACT FINDING: nextsearch/grading.py:592 _ws_number_near uses a RELATIVE tolerance, abs(r-t) <= abs(t)*criterion with criterion 0.05 = 5%. Ten of the eleven changed cells differ by under 1.2%, so they pass either way and the patch is a pure correctness cleanup there. Only 2022 (112.3 vs 101.5, 10.6% apart) actually flips grading - after the patch a model answering Nielsen's 101.5 is credited and NBC's 112.3 is not. That single high-stakes cell got the heaviest scrutiny and is right: NBC's 112.3M was a self-branded 'Total Audience Delivery' that summed 101.1M Nielsen TV viewers and 11.2M streamers rather than an average-minute audience, Nielsen's own headline was 'Super Bowl LVI Draws More Than 101 Million TV Viewers', and the gold's own 37.9 rating for 2022 is Nielsen's combined value, which pairs with 101.5 and not 112.3. On the 2019 rounding tie the auditor flagged: 98,950,000 is exactly 98.95, so 99.0 (half-up) vs 98.9 (half-even) is genuinely arbitrary, but both sit far inside the 5% tolerance so it is immaterial; 99.0 is the conventional choice and I accept it.
